strengths: Identifies and rigorously formalizes a previously under-appreciated failure mode—Marginal Path Collapse (MPC)—in ratio-of-densities steering of heterogeneous diffusion/flow experts, where the composed intermediate density becomes non-normalizable despite valid endpoints. This is a clear conceptual contribution with practical relevance.

Provides a sharp, well-proven Path Existence Criterion (Theorem 2.1, with sufficiency/necessity proofs in Theorem B.1 for compactly-supported targets and Theorem B.3 for Gaussian mixtures), giving a tractable, checkable condition based only on noise schedules and exponents.

The proposed Adaptive Path Correction with Exponents (ACE) is theoretically grounded: existence of a valid corrected exponent schedule is constructively proven (Theorem B.2/2.2), the corresponding weighted SDE/ODE sampling dynamics are rigorously derived via Itô's formula (Theorem A.1/2.3), and a concentration-control result (Proposition 2.1/E.1) connects the criterion to quantile-radius stabilization, giving mechanistic insight into why ACE improves sample quality.

Extensive, diverse empirical validation: a controlled synthetic checkerboard benchmark, a realistic flexible-pose scaffold decoration task composing three heterogeneous pretrained molecular experts, a fragment-linking task, and a homogeneous compositional image generation benchmark (COCO-MIG)—showing consistent improvements over FKC/NR baselines and competitive/superior performance versus specialized task-specific models (AutoFragDiff, Delete, FFLOM, GLIGEN).

Thorough sensitivity/ablation studies (bump hyperparameters B1/B2, ESS threshold, comparison against heuristic time-varying exponent schedules and against time-reparameterization alternatives), plus a systematic survey (Tables E.7-E.9) documenting that heterogeneous noise schedules are pervasive across published molecular generative models, strengthening the practical motivation.

Honest and well-organized discussion of scope and limitations (compact-support assumption, linear scaling with number of experts, restriction to steering rather than model correction, deferral of categorical/discrete variable extensions), and a reproducibility statement with code and fixed seeds.
weaknesses: The correction mechanism itself (bump function with hyperparameters B1, B2) is somewhat heuristic in how the added exponent perturbation is chosen; the theory guarantees existence of a valid path but not near-optimality relative to the original intended path, and the authors acknowledge that excessive correction can steer the path unnecessarily far from the desired trajectory.

Theoretical guarantees are largely restricted to Gaussian-to-compactly-supported interpolants (Theorem 2.1) or Gaussian mixture targets (Theorem B.3); extension to the mixed continuous-categorical domains that dominate real molecular generation (atom/bond types) is explicitly left to future work, somewhat limiting immediate end-to-end applicability despite the molecular experiments' apparent success.

Some real-data experiments have limited sample sizes (5 candidates per pocket, 66-76 pocket-ligand pairs) and modest reported margins in certain drug-likeness metrics (QED, SA, Lipinski often nearly tied across methods in Tables 3-4), making some of the practical gains for molecular design less dramatic than the synthetic and criterion-violation results would suggest.

The manuscript is extremely dense and heavily reliant on a 45-page appendix for core theoretical machinery (Theorem A.1, B.1-B.3) and most quantitative studies, which could hinder accessibility and independent verification without substantial cross-referencing effort.

While the diagnosis (Path Existence Criterion) is clearly novel, the correction algorithm builds closely on the existing Feynman-Kac corrector framework (Skreta et al., 2025a) by generalizing constant to time-varying exponents; the degree of technical novelty in the sampler itself, as opposed to the diagnostic criterion, is comparatively incremental.

strengths: Identifies a genuine and previously unformalized failure mode ('Marginal Path Collapse') in heterogeneous ratio-of-densities composition of diffusion/flow models with mismatched noise schedules, supported by a clean pedagogical Gaussian counterexample (Fig. 2/Eq. 3) and a rigorous survey (Appendix E.3, Tables E.7-E.9) showing that heterogeneous schedules are the norm rather than the exception across published molecular generative model families.

Provides a solid theoretical apparatus: a sharp sufficient/necessary Path Existence Criterion for compactly-supported targets (Theorem 2.1/B.1) and for Gaussian mixtures (Theorem B.3), a constructive existence proof for adaptive exponent schedules (Theorem B.2), and a full derivation of the corrected weighted SDE/ODE dynamics with importance weights (Theorem A.1/2.3), including a concentration-control result (Proposition 2.1/E.1) linking the criterion to quantile-radius control.

Extensive and fairly diverse empirical validation: a synthetic 2D checkerboard benchmark with systematic ablations over noise schedules and ESS thresholds, a full flexible-pose scaffold-decoration pipeline combining three pretrained molecular experts (DN/CONF/SBDD) evaluated against several strong baselines (FKC, NR, AutoFragDiff, Delete), a fragment-linking task compared against a task-specific model (FFLOM), and a homogeneous compositional image-generation benchmark (COCO-MIG) showing ACE also helps even without collapse.

Careful accounting of failure semantics: the paper clearly explains the subtle 'finite scores do not imply valid steering' phenomenon (Example A.1), which is a nuanced and important point that is easy to overlook and is well-illustrated theoretically and empirically.

Reasonably transparent reporting of limitations (Gaussian-to-compact-support assumption, linear scaling with number of experts, inapplicability to categorical/discrete variables, need for architecture-agnostic scope) and an extensive appendix with sensitivity analyses, comparisons to alternative fixes (time reparameterization), and future-work discussion.
weaknesses: The proposed correction (bump functions with hyperparameters B1, B2) is a heuristic patch layered on top of the rigorous existence theory; empirical sensitivity to these hyperparameters is substantial and non-monotonic (Tables C.2-C.5 show performance swinging considerably, sometimes degrading, as B1/B2 vary), which weakens the claim that ACE offers a principled, tuning-free solution and shows the 'guarantee' of path existence does not automatically translate into good sample quality without additional search.

The central drug-design motivation (structure-based/scaffold molecular generation) is validated only on continuous 3D coordinate diffusion; the theory and experiments explicitly avoid the categorical atom/bond-type variables that are integral to real molecular generative pipelines, with bonds inferred via a post-hoc geometric heuristic disconnected from the theoretical framework (acknowledged as future work in Appendix F), meaning the flagship scientific application is a simplification of the real problem.

Some key experiments have limited statistical rigor: the fragment-linking evaluation (Table E.6) is run with a single random seed, and the CrossDocked-based evaluations use relatively small test sets (76 and 66 complexes), which limits confidence in the significance of the reported gains for a paper emphasizing drug-design impact.

Baselines (NR/FKC) are, by the paper's own construction, guaranteed to fail whenever the path-existence criterion is violated, so much of the comparative improvement is somewhat definitional/by-design rather than reflecting a nontrivial modeling advance beyond adjusting exponents to satisfy C(t) > 0; the paper would benefit from more head-to-head comparison against simpler practical fixes (e.g., naive schedule normalization/matching) beyond the one time-reparameterization baseline included.

Reported molecular quality metrics are mixed rather than uniformly favorable: e.g., in Table 4, fixed-pose baselines (Delete/AutoFragDiff) sometimes achieve higher QED/SA than ACE despite ACE's better OSR/Vina scores, and the drug-likeness gains cited in the discussion section are somewhat overstated relative to the more mixed table values.

The manuscript is very long (60 pages with an extensive appendix) and defers many of the more substantive theoretical results (e.g., the GMM necessity theorem, the boundary-case analysis) entirely to the appendix, making the self-contained contribution of the main paper comparatively thin relative to the heuristic bump-function engineering that is the actually deployed fix.

strengths: Identifies a genuinely underappreciated failure mode, 'Marginal Path Collapse,' in heterogeneous ratio-of-densities composition, and provides a rigorous mathematical characterization (Path Existence Criterion, Theorem 2.1/B.1, extended to GMMs in B.3-B.4) that explains why constant-exponent steering and even existing Feynman-Kac correctors can silently produce samples from an unintended path despite numerically well-posed dynamics (nicely illustrated by the finite-score 'paradox' in Example A.1).

The proposed correction (ACE) is theoretically grounded rather than purely heuristic: existence of a valid corrected exponent schedule is proven constructively (Theorem 2.2/B.2), the corresponding weighted SDE/ODE sampling dynamics are derived via Itô calculus (Theorem A.1), and a concentration-control result (Proposition 2.1/E.1) gives a principled account of why the correction stabilizes sampling (quantile-radius shrinkage).

Extensive and diverse empirical validation: a synthetic checkerboard benchmark with closed-form ground truth, a realistic flexible-pose scaffold-decoration task with pretrained DN/CONF/SBDD experts, fragment linking, and a compositional image generation benchmark (COCO-MIG) in a homogeneous setting, each with sensible metrics (Vina score, QED/SA/Lipinski, OSR, W1/W2/MMD, CLIP, mIoU/attribute success).

Careful ablations and robustness checks: sensitivity to bump hyperparameters B1,B2 (Tables C.3-C.5, Fig. C.4), ESS threshold sensitivity (Fig. C.3), comparison against empirical time-varying exponent schedules and a time-reparameterization alternative (Appendix E.3, E.6), and a systematic survey (125 schedule combinations) showing collapse is prevalent (41-80% of heterogeneous compositions) rather than a rare edge case.

Good positioning relative to prior work: explicitly shows CFG, product-of-experts, reward-tilted guidance, and Bayesian composition are special cases of the ratio-of-densities template, and clarifies the precise relationship to and generalization of Feynman-Kac correctors (Skreta et al.).

Reasonably reproducible: exact noise-schedule formulas, hyperparameters, and algorithmic pseudocode (Algorithms 1-2) are provided, and the paper states code is released; compute resources and seeds are documented.

Honest and specific discussion of limitations and scope (Gaussian-to-compact-support interpolants only, linear cost scaling in number of experts, does not correct misaligned experts, does not yet address mixed continuous-categorical molecular representations) rather than glossing over them, plus a substantive 'Future Directions' section.
weaknesses: The paper is very dense and heavily backloaded into a 60-page appendix with many theorems/propositions/remarks; the main text sometimes states results 'informally' (e.g., Proposition 2.1) with the rigorous statement and proof relegated far away, which could hurt clarity for readers who don't traverse the full appendix.

Some key experiments rely on a single random seed or few seeds (e.g., fragment linking is run with a single seed; scaffold decoration ablations use 3 seeds), which limits the statistical confidence of comparisons against close competitors (e.g., FFLOM in Table E.6 is fairly competitive with ACE on some metrics).

The bump-function correction, while proven to exist and guarantee C(t)>0, still requires empirical hyperparameter search (B1, B2) for good sample quality/bias tradeoff; the theory guarantees validity but not optimality of the corrected path, and the sensitivity tables (C.3-C.5) show performance can degrade noticeably outside a fairly narrow 'stable region,' so practical tuning burden remains nontrivial despite the theoretical backing.

Current instantiations of the framework operate on molecules as point clouds (continuous coordinates only); extension to the mixed continuous-categorical representations that dominate real molecular generation (atom/bond/formal-charge types) is explicitly left as future work, somewhat limiting the immediate real-world applicability of the drug-design experiments.

ACE's inference cost scales linearly with the number of experts and requires log-density tracking/resampling machinery beyond standard guidance; while ACE-lite partially mitigates this, it reintroduces some bias and higher variance, so the practical efficiency-quality tradeoff is not fully resolved.

Comparisons to some task-specific baselines (e.g., GLIGEN in the COCO-MIG homogeneous experiment) show ACE only matching or exceeding on 'several' metrics rather than uniformly dominating, so the claimed generality of gains should be read with appropriate nuance rather than as a strict superiority result in every regime.
